# Condition Number as Digits Lost

"Ill-conditioned" is a word that does no work. The condition number turned into **decimal digits
of accuracy destroyed by the solve** is a number that does:

```
digits lost ≈ log₁₀(condition)
```

A double carries about sixteen. A system with condition `10¹⁰` returns an answer with roughly
six correct digits; at `10¹⁶` it returns none, and it returns them without complaint.

## The measurement that makes ridge regression obvious

Ridge adds `λI` to the Gram matrix before solving. That shifts every eigenvalue up by exactly
λ, which is why a singular system becomes solvable and a merely bad one becomes good. Measured
on a degree-8 polynomial design over eleven points:

| λ | condition estimate | digits lost |
|---:|---:|---:|
| 0 | 3.32 × 10¹⁰ | 10.5 |
| 10⁻⁸ | 1.07 × 10⁸ | 8.0 |
| 10⁻⁶ | 2.71 × 10⁶ | 6.4 |
| 10⁻⁴ | 4.57 × 10⁴ | 4.7 |
| 10⁻² | 7.78 × 10² | 2.9 |
| 1 | 1.01 × 10¹ | 1.0 |

Ten of sixteen digits gone before any regularisation. The λ that a model-selection sweep picks
on validation error is usually somewhere in the middle of that table, which means the stability
gain is real and not an artefact of a value nobody would choose.

## Polynomial fits are the standard bad case

A polynomial design matrix is a Vandermonde matrix, and Vandermonde matrices are the textbook
example of ill-conditioning. Anyone fitting a high-degree polynomial to closely spaced points is
in this regime by default, not by misfortune.

That is worth knowing because the symptom is not an error. The solve succeeds, the coefficients
come back finite, and they are wrong in the digits nobody prints.

## Solve, do not invert

`(ΦᵀΦ)⁻¹Φᵀy` is how the formula is written and `solve(ΦᵀΦ, Φᵀy)` is how it should be computed.
The two are algebraically identical; the explicit inverse does more arithmetic and keeps less of
it. On a Vandermonde system the difference is measurable rather than theoretical, which is why
both routes exist in the implementation and a test compares them.

## State the estimate's limits with the estimate

The implementation's `condition_estimate` is the ratio of largest to smallest pivot in the
elimination, not the true 2-norm condition number, which needs singular values. It tracks the
same thing closely enough to demonstrate the effect and it is named `condition_estimate` for
exactly that reason — [[provenance-and-limits-stated-inline]].

An approximation labelled as the real thing is a claim that will be relied on past its accuracy.

## The cost side

Regularisation buys stability with bias. On data an unregularised fit handles well, ridge makes
the training error strictly worse, and that is asserted rather than mentioned. λ is not a free
improvement; it is a dial between two failures, which is the same shape as
[[held-out-error-over-training-error]] — a metric that only improves is a metric that is not
measuring the trade.

## Where this appears

Implemented and measured in [[systems-analysis-and-decision-support]]. The singular case raises
rather than returning an arbitrary member of the solution set, which is the
[[tests-that-pass-for-the-wrong-reason]] argument applied to numerics: an arbitrary answer is
indistinguishable from a real one once it leaves the function.
